content.tldr: ZooKeeper historically managed Kafka cluster consensus and metadata, but has been replaced by KRaft (Kafka Raft), allowing Kafka to operate autonomously without ZooKeeper.
content.simple_explanation: In legacy Kafka architectures (prior to version 3.x), Apache ZooKeeper maintained cluster membership, elected the active Controller broker, and stored topic/partition metadata. This dual-system architecture created operational complexity and limited clusters to around 200,000 partitions due to metadata sync latency. KIP-500 introduced KRaft (Kafka Raft consensus protocol), which stores cluster metadata directly in an internal Kafka topic (`@metadata`), enabling sub-second failover and millions of partitions.
content.real_world_example: A ship captain: in legacy days, the ship needed a remote shore station (ZooKeeper) to approve every internal watch rotation; with KRaft, the ship's officers run an internal voting council right on board.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: ZooKeeper was fully removed in Kafka 4.0. Modern production deployments should run KRaft mode exclusively for simplified operations and faster controller recovery.
